articles.author: Priyam
articles.description:
We’ve spent a lot of time talking about text hallucinations.
In vision-language systems, hallucination isn’t about plausible lies.
Examples:
Describing people who aren’t there
Assigning attributes that don’t exist
Inferring actions that never happened
As these models are deployed for:
E-commerce product listings
…the cost of hallucination changes from “wrong answer” to “real-world consequence.”
The issue is that most evaluation pipelines are still text-first.
Image hallucination requires multimodal evaluation:
Compare generated text against visual evidence
Reason about object presence, attributes, and relationships
Detect contradictions between image and output
This isn’t a niche problem.
Curious how others are approaching hallucination detection for image-based systems.
articles.title: Why Image Hallucination Is More Dangerous Than Text Hallucination

articles.author: Om Shree
articles.description:
Navigating a binary tree can often feel like exploring a multi-story building. To find which floor has the most "value," we need a strategy that lets us visit one level at a time and tally up the scores.
You're given:
The root of a binary tree where each node contains an integer value.
A structure where the root starts at Level 1, its children are at Level 2, and so on.
Your goal:
Find the level number that has the highest total sum of node values.
If two or more levels have the same maximum sum, return the smallest (lowest) level number among them.
For Example

Input: root = [1,7,0,7,-8,null,null]
The most effective way to process a tree level by level is a technique called Breadth-First Search (BFS). Instead of diving deep into one branch, we use a queue to keep track of all nodes on the…
articles.title: 🌲 Beginner-Friendly Guide 'Maximum Level Sum of a Binary Tree' – LeetCode 1161 (C++, Python, JavaScript)

articles.description:
When we started building Bifrost, we assumed load balancing for LLM requests would work like traditional API load balancing. Configure some fallback rules, set priority orders, maybe add weighted routing. Ship it.
That assumption lasted about three weeks into production.
The problem became obvious during the first major provider incident we experienced. OpenAI didn't just "go down." Instead, one region started timing out. Then another spiked with 5xx errors. Latency drifted upward across certain endpoints while others worked fine. By the time it became a full incident, half our traffic had already degraded for 20 minutes.
Our carefully configured fallback rules - rate limits, cost priorities, manual route ordering - sat there doing nothing useful. They were designed for clean failures: pro…

Delayed sourcing cycles
Increased internal coordination costs
When vendor discovery lacks structure, procurement teams end up paying for inefficiency instead of value.
